newsitem.title: GERMANY: Spiegel says Tietmeyer asks about EMU delay option.
newsitem.headline: Spiegel says Tietmeyer asks about EMU delay option.

text.p: Germany's Der Spiegel magazine said on Saturday that Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer had asked whether Germany and France could consider delaying European monetary union (EMU).
"Wouldn't it be a possibility, together with France, to agree to a delay in the start of the euro?" the magazine quoted Tietmeyer as saying in an article to be published on Monday.
But German Finance Minister Theo Waigel responded by saying it was counterproductive to discuss a delay to EMU, which is set for January 1, 1999.
Spiegel, citing unnamed sources, said Tietmeyer did not believe it would be wrong if currency union were delayed if Bonn and Paris did not meet the entry criteria this year.
The Maastricht Treaty has requirements on budget deficits and debts, interest rates, inflation and foreign exchange rates that must be met in 1997 to join currency union at the start.
Waigel said on Saturday that a delay to EMU would only unsettle financial markets. He also said any delay must be agreed by the European Union council of ministers.
"It does not make sense to discuss a delay in currency union," Waigel told reporters at an outing in Bavaria.
A Spiegel spokesman said the magazine had not spoken directly with Tietmeyer, saying the information was based on talks with sources in Germany. He declined further comment.
A Bundesbank spokesman could not immediately be reached for comment on the Spiegel article.

Prospects for a delay have risen after Bonn and the Bundesbank openly clashed over a plan by Waigel to revalue the bank's reserves and demand a payout of the hidden profits to help Bonn cut its budget deficit.

The Bundesbank, a fierce advocate of fiscal austerity and opponent of tricks in meeting criteria for monetary union, on Wednesday criticised Waigel's plan and said it could undermine the new currency, the euro, from the start.

The row prompted the leader of Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to call on Chancellor Helmut Kohl to call a general election, saying the government's plan to revalue gold reserves was damaging Bonn's credibility.

"The economic and finance policies of the Kohl government have failed. The coalition is so split it's not capable of acting. It would be good for Germany if it cleared the path for fresh elections," SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said in the interview released on Saturday with Der Spiegel.

German central bank sources have said in the past that the question of delaying the union should not be a total taboo if either Germany or France, considered crucial members, failed to meet entry criteria in the treaty.
Tietmeyer has not made the case in the past for a delay in currency union but has simply asked the question as to whether this should be considered, bank sources have said.
Tietmeyer has not commented publicly on the row over the revaluation of reserves since the bank issued a statement on Wednesday criticising Waigel's plan.
But he is expected to strongly oppose the plan in a meeting scheduled for next week with Bonn lawmakers in parliament's finance committee.
Kohl's government plans to introduce legislation next week to change Bundesbank laws and allow for the transfer of the extra profits despite the central bank's objection.

Experts said Tietmeyer may see reason for a delay in the union if German finances were not stable in a sustainable way. But they noted Kohl has enough votes to get the Bundesbank proposal, as well as final approval for EMU, passed in parliament.
Waigel has said his plan to revalue reserves does not attack the Bundesbank's independence and that the bank agreed with him on the need to value the gold and currency reserves towards market prices.
He has said the bank's only point of contention was whether the reserves would be revalued in 1997, or in 1999 as the bank prefers.
